lead: The Saturday at the base starts at a desk, and what you sign there decides who pays for what on Friday. Your contract and the base's briefing are the authority; this is how they usually read.

sections.title: What the desk asks for and what sails with you

qa.q: What documents do I need to pick up a bareboat charter yacht?
qa.a: The base checks the **skipper's licence** and a VHF operator's certificate, which may be a crew member's, and files a crew list with everyone's passport details for the port police.

blocks.p: The base checks the **skipper's licence** and a **VHF operator's certificate**, and files a **crew list** with passport details for the port police. A licence the base cannot accept means no bareboat: a licensed crew member is named as skipper, or the base supplies one. Only a skipper named in the contract may be in command; anyone may steer under them. A co-skipper is added, licence shown, before you sign. The radio certificate may be a crew member's.

blocks.p: Everyone who sleeps aboard is on the crew list, children included; a change mid-week is reported to the base. The boat's licence limits the **persons aboard** under way: a day guest counts.

sections.title: What the deposit covers and what it does not

qa.q: Is the charter deposit actually taken from my card?
qa.a: Usually not: on a card it is a **pre-authorisation**, the sum blocked, not taken, and released after a clean check-out. It caps what you pay for insured damage; what the contract excludes stays with you.

blocks.p: The **deposit** is your limit for insured damage to the boat. On a card it is a pre-authorisation: the sum is blocked, not taken, and released after a clean check-out. It is in place in full before the keys change hands; a second card or cash against a receipt gets round a card limit.

blocks.p: The price normally includes the base's own berth only: harbour fees, fuel and food are the crew's.

sections.title: Where, when and how you may sail

qa.q: Am I allowed to sail at night on a bareboat charter?
qa.a: Usually not: a bareboat contract normally forbids **night sailing** and sailing above a stated wind, inside a named cruising area. Outside these limits the insurance and the deposit limit can fall away.

blocks.p: A bareboat contract names a **cruising area**, usually forbids sailing at night and above a stated wind, and may list harbours you must not enter. Outside these limits the insurance and the deposit limit can fall away. Only the base moves a limit, in writing, before you go. For shelter it can allow a forbidden harbour; held in port by the wind limit, you agree the return with the base.

fig.title: Will you be in before sunset?

blocks.p: Racing, towing another vessel and paying passengers are normally excluded and uninsured. Your duty at sea is to people in danger: stand by a disabled yacht, relay her call, and tow only if she is in immediate danger. A pet aboard, or a different return base on a one-way charter, needs the base's consent in advance.

sections.title: Local knowledge no pilot book has

qa.q: What should I write down at the charter base briefing?
qa.a: The **chart briefing**: the base's knowledge of its own waters, such as the reef to keep off, the quay with ferry wash, the bay where gusts fall at night. Write it on your chart; it outranks a calm evening.

blocks.p: The **chart briefing** is the base's experience of its own waters: the reef to keep off, the quay with ferry wash, the bay where gusts fall from the cliffs after dark. Write it on your chart as the manager speaks. When a quay attendant or a calm evening says otherwise, the briefing wins.

fig.note: Briefing: E bay, night gusts in a northerly

blocks.cap: A is calm at 18:00, not at night: anchor at B.

blocks.p: The **technical briefing** is done aboard, hands on: every charter boat is wired and plumbed differently. Keep a second crew member with you and brief the rest yourself that evening; someone else checks the provisioning delivery against the order.

sections.title: The paper the deposit is settled against

qa.q: When should I sign the check-in form on a charter yacht?
qa.a: Only after the walk-round, with what you found written in and countersigned by the base. Anything not on the **check-in form** counts as new damage at check-out, so you pay for it.

blocks.p: The **check-in form** records the boat as you took her over; anything not on it counts as new damage at check-out. So you sign the contract at the desk, but the form only after the walk-round, with what you found written in and countersigned by the base. On a busy Saturday it is still your walk-round. A late arrival is agreed in advance: walk-round, form and briefing then happen next morning, before you leave.

blocks.rule: What is not written, located, measured and countersigned before you sign is yours to pay for.

sections.title: Report at once, come back on time

qa.q: What do I do if I damage the charter boat during the week?
qa.a: Report it to the base **at once** and don't sail on with it: the base decides the repair. After a collision take no cash; note the other boat's name, port and insurer, and photograph everything.

blocks.p: The **named skipper** answers to the base for the boat, whoever was steering. Under the contract you report a fault or damage **at once** and do not sail on with it: the base decides the repair. A grounding found only at check-out is treated as hidden. After a collision take no cash: note the other boat's name, port and insurer, photograph everything and call the base: insurers settle it.

fig.note: Full to full: A first, then B

blocks.p: The boat is due in the base marina the evening before check-out, tanks full: refuelling by the base costs extra. Coming back early is your call: no refund, and tell the base. A late return is charged by the hour. Small allowances, such as one empty gas bottle, are in the contract too.
